name: Kira Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you tell me is confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a blast-hole drill rig at an open-pit iron ore mine, and I lead the drill crew on day shift, six of us. We get the drill pattern from the engineers, then I position the rig and drill holes about fifteen metres deep for the blasting crew. Most of my day is in the cab watching the pressure and the penetration rate, which tells me what the rock is doing. I work for a drilling contractor, not the mine itself, so the pay is lower than the mine's own people.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the rig talks to you if you listen. I use an AI app every day to sort my drill logs and spot which holes went soft, and the engineers actually ask me for it now. What wears me out is the money. I'm paying off my diploma loan and helping my little brother through uni, so I've got maybe three weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So my little log tricks are about as far as it goes. Fair enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a handy helper, not a revolution, and I'd keep showing the crew how I use it. At work I'd say the real fight is still contractor pay. Online I'd probably post something about how hype helps share prices more than workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed. I was hoping the tech would open up something better for me than the same cab for twenty years. My job's safe, but I'd still be broke on contractor rates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling and keep building my log tools, and pitch them to the contractor as a way to cut re-drills. I'd ask the union about getting contractor drillers on the mine's agreement. And I'd do a short online course in data analysis at night, just because I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine but restless. It's not fear, it's itchy feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you pitched the log tools and they said yes, would you want paying for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd want a pay bump or a new title, not just a pat on the back. Last time I fixed something, the supervisor put it in his report as his idea. I wouldn't let that happen twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if your brother needed more money one month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd send it and eat rice for a week. He's the first in our family at university and I'm not going to be the reason he drops out. That's the deal I made with Mum.

The real fight is still **contractor pay**, and hype mainly helps share prices.
think: I'm **disappointed** the tech won't open up something better than the same cab.
My job's safe, but I'm still **broke** on contractor rates.
do: **Pitch** her drill-log tool to the contractor to cut re-drills.
Ask the union to put contractor drillers on the **mine's agreement**.
Take a short **data analysis** course at night.
feel: **Restless**, with itchy feet rather than fear.
S0.quote: I was hoping the tech would open up something better for me than the same cab for twenty years.
fieldNote: She is the rare miner **disappointed** that AI is only hype.
Her money squeeze comes from a **diploma loan** and supporting her brother.
She wants **credit and pay** for her ideas after a past slight.

steps.text: Pitch her drill-log AI tool to cut re-drills
Ask the union to cover contractor drillers under the mine's agreement
Take an online data analysis course at night

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one I can work with. The mine already has two autonomous drills on trial in the north pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should get ahead of it, not hide from it. At work I'd put my hand up to supervise the autonomous drills. At union meetings I'd argue for a deal where the savings pay for training, not just dividends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine, maybe better off. Someone has to set the patterns, watch four rigs on a screen and walk out when one gets stuck. The people I'd worry about are the drillers who won't touch the tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a transfer to the autonomous drill trial within a month. I'd use AI tools to learn the fleet software before the training even starts. And I'd push the union to get a written promise that drillers get first pick of the new jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, and a bit guilty about being excited. My crew won't all make it across.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel guilty. Who on your crew are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gus, who's been drilling longer than I've been alive and hates screens. He taught me to hear when a bit is about to go. I'd try to get him into training the new crews on rock, because the computer still doesn't know rock like he does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would supervising four rigs pay more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It should, but with contractors you never know. If they tried to keep the same rate for four times the rigs, I'd make a fuss. That's where the union comes in.

say: People should **get ahead** of the change, not hide from it.
Automation savings should pay for **training**, not just dividends.
think: I'd probably be **fine**, supervising several rigs from a screen.
I worry about drillers who **won't touch** the tablet.
do: Ask for a **transfer** to the autonomous drill trial within a month.
Use **AI tools** to learn the fleet software before training starts.
Push for a **written promise** that drillers get first pick of new jobs.
feel: **Excited**, and guilty that her crew won't all make it across.
S1.quote: Someone has to set the patterns, watch four rigs on a screen and walk out when one gets stuck.
fieldNote: She sees the drill **trial** as her way up, not a threat.
Her guilt over **Gus** shows she knows adaptation isn't open to everyone.
She still relies on the **union** to make sure new jobs are paid fairly.

steps.text: Request a transfer to the autonomous drill trial in the north pit

Get a written union promise that drillers get first pick

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That kills the plan I just gave you, doesn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for any town to handle, and government has to step in with income support and a say in how it's rolled out. At work I'd tell people to stop waiting for someone to fix it. Online I'd be loud about who gets the profits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the supervising job I wanted is thinking work, so it goes in 2028. My hands-on drilling would last until about 2031. So I'd have three years in a cab I was trying to get out of, then nothing at this mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop chasing the screen job and look for work that mixes hands and judgement, like maintaining the robot rigs. I'd try to get a job with the company that makes the autonomous drills, even if it meant moving to the city. And I'd use every AI tool I can to learn their systems fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Being early to new tech doesn't help much when the tech can do the learning faster than you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving to the city on three weeks of savings, how would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be hard. I'd couch-surf at a friend's place for the first month and keep sending my brother what I could. I'd only go once I had an offer in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd want the union involved. What would you want them to fight for here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A share of the savings for every worker the robots replace, paid for a few years. And a say in which pits go first. Otherwise it's just shareholders taking everything.

I'd be loud online about **who gets the profits**.

steps.text: Apply for robot-rig maintenance jobs at the drill maker

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to make one big move, if I start straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so let's not waste it. At work I'd start a lunchtime group to show people the AI tools. At the union I'd say we need retraining money in the next deal, not the one after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have time to get a proper qualification, maybe an electrical trade or mechatronics, which is the mix of electrics and mechanics in robots. That would put me in the maintenance crew when the robots arrive in 2034. It's not safe forever, but it's longer than driving a rig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enrol in a part-time mechatronics certificate within six months, online with a few block weeks in the city. I'd keep drilling full time to pay for it. I'd run the lunchtime AI group for my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but in charge. Like the night before an exam you've actually studied for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you afford the course on three weeks of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mine has a training fund that hardly anyone uses, I'd apply for it. If that fails, I'd pay it off monthly and skip my holiday. My brother finishes uni in two years, which frees up a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Gus, the old driller, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him he has time to finish his career on the rig and he shouldn't let anyone rush him out. Then I'd ask him to teach the lunchtime group about rock. He'd grumble, but he'd turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years for the thinking side and thirteen for robots. That's a whole career change with room to spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so governments and companies should use it to share the gains. At work I'd keep pushing for training to be part of every pay deal. Online I'd be less angry and more practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty good about it. I'd finish the mechatronics course, then maybe an engineering degree part time. My bigger worry would be money in the next couple of years, not robots in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the mechatronics course first, then see. I'd move into the autonomous drill trial as soon as it opens. And I'd use the AI tools to help me study, same as I do now with the logs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. A bit impatient, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said money worries you more than robots here. What would ease that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting on the mine's own payroll instead of the contractor's is about a fifteen percent jump. I'd chase that before anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be at the same mine in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, and that's okay. I'd follow the work, maybe to a remote operations centre in the city. My mum would hate it, but she'd get over it.

say: Ten years is a **gift**, and the gains should be shared.
**Training** should be part of every pay deal.
think: I'd feel **good**, with time for mechatronics and maybe an engineering degree.
My bigger worry is **money** in the next two years, not robots.
do: Move into the **autonomous drill trial** when it opens.
S4.quote: Getting on the mine's own payroll instead of the contractor's is about a fifteen percent jump.
fieldNote: Ten years makes her **hopeful**, even eager.
Her near-term focus is moving off **contractor pay**.

steps.text: Apply for a job on the mine's own payroll

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'm usually the one who loves new tech, but two years means the screen jobs go just as I get to them, and the robots come for the rig three years later. What would help is a real retraining payment, so someone on three weeks of savings can study without starving, and a union deal that shares the savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who's already using these tools. Lots of miners like me use AI every day and nobody asks us how to roll it out. We'd do it better than head office.

headlineQuote: Lots of miners like me use AI every day and nobody asks us how to roll it out. We'd do it better than head office.
portrait: Kira is a **27-year-old** drill crew lead at an open-pit iron ore mine, paid at contractor rates.
She uses **AI daily** for drill logs and has about three weeks of savings.
She is **pro-union** and wants automation savings shared with workers.
In slower pictures she sees **opportunity**, aiming for autonomous drills and a mechatronics trade.
AGI by 2028 leaves her **alarmed**, because the screen jobs vanish just as she reaches them.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028**, when the screen jobs vanish just as she gets to them.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining payment** so workers with little savings can study.
A **union deal** that shares automation savings with workers.
